nameStory: This aquatic plant earned its "broad-leaved" name from having some of the widest leaves among all the pondweeds in New England. While many of its relatives have narrow, grass-like leaves, this species stands out with leaves that can stretch up to 3 inches wide. The name helps botanists and nature lovers quickly distinguish it from the many other pondweed species that share our lakes and ponds.
description: Broad-leaved pondweed is an aquatic plant that lives completely in the water of lakes, ponds, and rivers throughout New England. It grows from underground stems called rhizomes and can reach up to 3 feet long with very slender, cylindrical stems. This perennial plant produces two different types of leaves - some that stay underwater and others that float on the surface - along with spikes of small flowers that rise above the water.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Two distinct leaf types: underwater leaves up to 8 inches long and 3 inches wide that feel thin and may fold along their center line, plus smaller floating leaves that feel leathery and thick between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense spikes of tiny greenish flowers held above the water surface on thick, sturdy stalks that feel firm when gently touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Very slender, smooth stems that feel almost wire-like and may show dark spots, growing completely submerged except for the flower spikes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Underwater leaves have an unusually high number of parallel veins (up to 49) that you can see when holding a leaf up to the light

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Floating leaves are attached to long leaf stalks (petioles) that feel smooth and allow the leaves to bob on the water surface

habitat: Look for broad-leaved pondweed in deeper areas of lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers throughout New England. It thrives in clear to moderately clear water and often grows alongside other aquatic plants like water lilies and other pondweed species. You'll typically find it in waters 3-15 feet deep where it can anchor its roots in muddy or sandy bottoms.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from overwintering rhizomes, with fresh underwater leaves appearing first as water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with both underwater and floating leaves fully developed, and flower spikes rising above the water surface from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to die back and flower spikes may persist into early fall, with seeds dispersing in the water.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back completely, with only the underground rhizome system surviving beneath the ice until spring.

funFact: Broad-leaved pondweed is like an underwater chameleon - it can completely change its leaf shape depending on water conditions! In deeper, calmer water it produces those characteristic broad floating leaves, but in shallower or more turbulent areas, it might only make the narrow underwater leaves, making it look like a completely different plant.
confusionNotes: It's most easily confused with floating-leaved pondweed, but broad-leaved pondweed has much wider underwater leaves and more veins in each leaf. Remember: "broad" means both the underwater AND floating leaves are wider than most other pondweeds - if you only see narrow underwater leaves, it's probably a different species.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name Potamogeton comes from Greek words meaning "river" and "neighbor," reflecting these plants' aquatic lifestyle. With over 20 pondweed species in New England, they're one of our most diverse groups of aquatic plants, though many look very similar and require close examination to identify correctly.
compareHints: Among New England's many pondweeds, broad-leaved pondweed is distinguished by having some of the widest underwater leaves with the most veins. Floating-leaved pondweed has similar floating leaves but much narrower underwater leaves, while ribbon-leaved pondweed lacks the broad floating leaves entirely. The high vein count in the underwater leaves (up to 49 veins) is a key feature that separates it from most other pondweeds.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many pondweeds, ribbon-leaved pondweed stands out for its distinctly long, narrow leaves that are much more ribbon-like than grass-like.

Among New England's many pondweeds, floating-leaved pondweed is unique in having large, obvious floating leaves - most other pondweeds have only thin underwater leaves or much smaller floating leaves.

Unlike floating-leaved pondweed which has oval leaves that float on the surface, or ribbon-leaved pondweed with its narrow straight leaves, curly-leaf pondweed's leaves stay completely underwater and have those unmistakable wavy, crimped edges.
Unlike ribbon-leaved and floating-leaved pondweeds which produce leaves that reach the water surface, Robbins' pondweed stays completely submerged throughout its life cycle.
Unlike floating-leaved pondweed which has leaves that float on the surface, perfoliate pondweed stays completely submerged.
Among New England's many pondweed species, longleaf pondweed stands out for having both underwater and floating leaves on long stalks - most relatives specialize in just one leaf type.

Among the pondweeds, Richardson's stands out for its relatively broad, crinkly-edged underwater leaves - much wider than grass-leaved or ribbon-leaved pondweed, but not as broad as the truly wide-leaved species like broad-leaved pondweed.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, spiral pondweed is unique for its twisted flower spikes – no other pondweed has this corkscrew feature.
Among New England's many pondweed species, grass-leaved pondweed stands out for its consistently narrow, grass-like submerged leaves that vary in length on the same plant.
Among the many New England pondweeds, eel-grass pondweed stands out for its extremely narrow, ribbon-like leaves that never float on the surface.
Among New England's many pondweeds, snailseed pondweed is most similar to other narrow-leaved species like Berchtold's and small pondweed, sharing the thin, linear leaves and small stature.

Berchtold's pondweed stands out from other New England pondweeds by having the narrowest leaves in the genus - much thinner than the ribbon-like leaves of ribbon-leaved pondweed or the broader blades of floating-leaved pondweed.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, white-stemmed pondweed is distinguished by its pale stems and preference for deeper, clearer water.

Among New England's pondweeds, Oakes' stands out for its extremely narrow, delicate leaves that are much thinner than the ribbon-like leaves of grass-leaved pondweed or the broader leaves of floating-leaved species.
Among New England's many pondweed species, spotted pondweed is the only one with translucent windows in its leaves.

Among New England's many pondweeds, leafy pondweed stands out for its extremely thin, hair-like leaves - much finer than broad-leaved pondweed's oval leaves or curly-leaf pondweed's wavy, serrated foliage.
Among New England's many pondweeds, Bluntleaf Pondweed stands out for its consistently blunt leaf tips, while most others like Ribbon-leaved Pondweed have pointed tips.
Among its many pondweed relatives, small pondweed stands out for having the most thread-like, delicate leaves - much thinner than grass-leaved pondweed or spiral pondweed.
Among New England's many pondweeds, northern pondweed stands out with its reddish stem coloration - most other species like ribbon-leaved pondweed or grass-leaved pondweed have plain green stems.
Among the many pondweed species in New England, Hill's pondweed stands out for its strict requirement for alkaline water and its rarity.

Among all the pondweeds, this species stands out for having by far the thinnest leaves – other pondweeds have ribbon-like, oval, or broader linear leaves, but none approach the hair-fine texture of Algae-like Pondweed.
Among New England's many pondweed species, shining pondweed stands out for its consistently glossy leaves - most other pondweeds have matte or only slightly shiny foliage.
Among the thin-leaved pondweeds, Vasey's pondweed is distinguished by very specific technical features of its fruits and stipules (small leaf-like structures at the leaf base).

Among New England's many pondweed species, Straightleaf Pondweed stands out for its rigid, upright leaf posture - most other pondweeds have either floating leaves, wavy underwater leaves, or much more flexible foliage.
